transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
More than 10,000 flights are delayed or cancelled today,
according to Flight Tracker FlightAware,
as thousands of passengers are still stranded
after yesterday's hours-long ground stop.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says a federal contractor
who's changing out copper wire for fiber optics may be to blame.
Former DOT Inspector General Mary Schiavo says
the contractor was doing software patches work,
which caused the system to reboot, resulting in the crash.
She says it was running on a router made some 20 years ago.
This has happened before, and most coincidentally,
or rather as in reading a crystal ball,
the Government Accountability Office on September 14, 2026
predicted exactly this.
They said without some major change,
the FAA will once again repeat its history
of cost overruns and missed deadlines.
Speaking there to NPR's Weekend Edition.
Some Republican state officials are trying to revive
the Trump administration's push for mail-in voting restrictions
for the 2028 election.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang has more.
More than a week after voting ended for this year's midterms,
Missouri's state Attorney General is leading 11 other
Republican state officials in this push to shape
the next federal election in 2028.
The U.S. Postal Service issued a revised mail-in ballot rule
in August in response to an executive order
by President Trump.
Under that rule, USPS would refuse to deliver
mail-in ballots to voters in states where election officials
do not turn over their voter list to the mailing agency.
The Supreme Court blocked the USPS rule for the midterms.
Now these Republican state officials are appealing
a lower court order that's blocking USPS from working
on the rule for the 2028 election.
U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols issued that order
after finding that the Postal Service likely has no
authority to impose these requirements on states.
The Trump administration is not appealing the order.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
A small makeshift memorial is steadily growing near
the Brooklyn apartment building that collapsed,
killing eight people in injury more than a dozen.
NPR's Duwakkalee Saikato has more.
Neighbors and visitors passing by here have been leaving
flowers, stuffed animals and candles.
They take photos and stare at what's left of a three-store
apartment building.
The exposed rooms reveal clothes still hanging in a closet.
A child's bike on the second floor.
Someone's dresser.
Winslet Etienne, who lives nearby, says city leaders
are not considering the needs of everyone.
I'm leaving a black building.
They don't care about black people.
That's all.
Men don't have to focus because we pay taxes like everybody
pays taxes.
The collapsed building is next to a major construction
site.
The investigation into the cause of that collapse is ongoing.
Duwakkalee Saikato, NPR News in Brooklyn.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Authorities in Hungary have recovered nearly $20 million
in cash allegedly hidden by a former government official.
Terry Schultz reports the investigation comes as the
country is cracking down on corruption after 16 years
under ousted Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Some of the millions of dollars of banknotes were
buried in forests.
Some were stashed in warehouses and farm buildings
across Hungary.
The man accused of stealing the money is Miklos Sestak,
the former development minister now accused of taking
illegal payments as part of transportation contracts.
The finance ministry says it took a dozen state treasury
workers eight hours using banknote counters to tally
up all the recovered cash.
Sestak has been in custody since September.
Two other former ministers, as well as Viktor Orban's
brother, have been arrested in separate corruption cases
as the effort to clean up the country's bureaucracy
gathers pace under Prime Minister Peter Magyar.
He took power from Orban in April and has pledged to
improve relations with the European Union.
For NPR News, I'm Terry Schultz in Brussels.
A popular Thanksgiving staple has been voluntarily
recalled because it might contain a cleaning chemical.
Almond's Foods says it's recalling cans of Kirkland
Signature heavy whipped cream, which is sold at Costco
stores in 12 states.
They say it was sold in three packs of 15-ounce cans.
Almond's says it voluntarily issued the recall after
learning that one batch may contain a small amount of
cleaning chemical, but it didn't identify what the
chemical is that is involved.
You're listening to NPR News.

topics.text: More than 10,000 flights delayed or canceled after yesterday's hours-long FAA ground stop
Duffy blames federal contractor's fiber optic work, with GAO having warned of FAA failures
Missouri AG leads Republican officials appealing ruling that blocks USPS mail-in ballot rule for 2028
Makeshift memorial grows near Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people
Hungary recovers nearly $20 million in cash allegedly hidden by former minister Miklos Sestak
Almond's Foods recalls Kirkland Signature heavy whipping cream sold at Costco over possible cleaning chemical
